concepts.name: Constitutional Basis and Scope of Governor's Ordinance Power (Article 213)
key_dimensions: Conditions precedent: Legislature not in session + immediate action necessary
Comparison with President's ordinance power under Article 123 — similarities and critical differences
Subjects on which Governor CAN vs CANNOT promulgate ordinances (State List, Concurrent List limitations)
UPSC trap: Governor cannot promulgate ordinance on matters requiring Presidential assent for a Bill

concepts.name: Governor's Satisfaction vs. Council of Ministers' Aid and Advice in Ordinance Promulgation
key_dimensions: Whether Governor can act independently of Cabinet advice while promulgating ordinances
44th Amendment and judicial position on 'satisfaction' being non-justiciable vs. D.C. Wadhwa case shift
Post-44th Amendment: Is Governor's satisfaction truly personal or bound by ministerial advice?
UPSC trap: Unlike certain discretionary powers, ordinance promulgation is generally on Cabinet advice

concepts.name: Limitations on Governor's Ordinance Power: Matters Requiring Presidential Assent
key_dimensions: Article 213(1) proviso: Categories of Bills that require prior Presidential instruction before ordinance
Three specific categories — Bills affecting High Court powers, compulsory acquisition of property, trade/commerce restrictions
Comparison: Same restrictions apply to corresponding Bills under Articles 200 and 304
UPSC trap: 'Prior instructions of the President' vs. 'previous sanction' — precise constitutional language

concepts.name: Life, Lapse, and Withdrawal of Governor's Ordinance
key_dimensions: Maximum operative period: 6 weeks from reassembly of Legislature — not 6 months like a common misconception
Three modes of cessation: expiry of 6 weeks, disapproval by Legislature, withdrawal by Governor
UPSC trap: Ordinance can be withdrawn by Governor at any time — no requirement of legislative approval for withdrawal
What happens if only one House disapproves in a bicameral state legislature?

concepts.name: Re-promulgation of Ordinances: Constitutional Validity and Judicial Scrutiny
key_dimensions: D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987): Supreme Court ruling against 'ordinance raj' and re-promulgation as fraud on Constitution
Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017): Nine-judge bench — re-promulgation without legislative approval is unconstitutional
Distinction between re-promulgation per se and re-promulgation to bypass legislature
UPSC trap: Court did NOT say re-promulgation is always void — context and intent matter

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Governor's Ordinance: Justiciability and Grounds
key_dimensions: A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982): Presidential/Governor's satisfaction not completely immune from judicial review
Krishna Kumar Singh (2017): Ordinances are subject to judicial review for malafides and constitutional limitations
Grounds of challenge: Lack of immediate necessity, mala fide intent, subject outside competence
UPSC trap: Ordinances have the same force as an Act of Legislature but are NOT Acts — distinction matters for immunity

concepts.name: Governor's Discretionary Powers: Constitutional Framework (Article 163)
key_dimensions: Article 163(1): Governor acts on aid and advice EXCEPT where he is 'required by or under the Constitution to exercise functions in his discretion'
Article 163(2): Governor's decision on whether a matter falls within discretion is FINAL and validity cannot be questioned
Article 163(3): Questions of advice tendered by Council of Ministers cannot be inquired into any court
UPSC trap: Discretion is the exception, not the rule — most functions are on ministerial advice

concepts.name: Enumerated Discretionary Powers of Governor
key_dimensions: Appointment of CM when no party has clear majority (hung assembly) — most significant discretionary power
Dismissal of Council of Ministers that has lost majority but refuses to resign or seek floor test
Dissolution of Assembly on advice of CM who has lost majority — Governor can refuse such advice
Reservation of Bill for President's consideration under Article 200 — Governor's subjective judgment
UPSC trap: Sending report to President under Article 356 — discretionary but heavily convention-bound post-Bommai

concepts.name: Governor's Role in Government Formation: Hung Assembly Scenarios
key_dimensions: Order of preference: Party/alliance with majority → pre-poll alliance → single largest party → post-poll alliance
Sarkaria Commission and Punchhi Commission guidelines on government formation
Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006): Governor cannot be partisan; floor test is the ultimate test
UPSC trap: Governor invites vs. Governor appoints — Constitutional language is 'appoints' (Article 164)

concepts.name: Reservation of Bills for Presidential Consideration (Article 200)
key_dimensions: Article 200: Four options available to Governor — assent, withhold assent, return for reconsideration, reserve for President
Mandatory reservation: Bills that derogate from High Court powers (Article 200 proviso)
Discretionary reservation vs. mandatory reservation — constitutional distinction
UPSC trap: Governor has NO time limit specified for reserving a bill, unlike withholding/returning — recent controversy in Supreme Court (2024 Tamil Nadu Governor case)

concepts.name: Governor's Assent to Bills: Constitutional Options and Limitations
key_dimensions: Unlike President under Article 111, Governor CANNOT exercise pocket veto for ordinary Bills (no time limit for return, but convention exists)
If Legislature re-passes the bill with or without amendments, Governor is bound to give assent — no second veto
UPSC trap: Governor withholding assent vs. reserving for President — different constitutional consequences
Supreme Court 2024 ruling (Tamil Nadu case): Governor cannot indefinitely withhold/sit on Bills — amounts to constitutional impropriety

concepts.name: Governor's Role Under President's Rule (Article 356): Powers and Accountability
key_dimensions: Governor's report under Article 356 — quasi-judicial character post-S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
S.R. Bommai case: Floor of the House is the only place to test majority; President's Rule subject to judicial review
Governor acts as agent of Centre during President's Rule — distinction from normal times
UPSC trap: Even during President's Rule, certain High Court powers/judicial functions remain independent

concepts.name: Appointment and Removal of Governor: Constitutional Position and Conventions
key_dimensions: Article 155 and 156: Appointed by President, holds office 'during pleasure of President' — no security of tenure like judges
Sarkaria Commission recommendation: Governor should not be removed arbitrarily; should be given reasonable opportunity
B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010): President cannot remove Governor without cause; removal must not be arbitrary/malafide
UPSC trap: 5-year term is conventional, NOT constitutional — Governor can be removed before that

concepts.name: Governor as Chancellor of State Universities: Nature of this Role
key_dimensions: Statutory role under state university acts — NOT a constitutional role unlike other powers
Recent controversies: West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala — state governments attempting to replace Governor as Chancellor
Governor acting independently vs. on ministerial advice in university matters — gray area
UPSC trap: This role is NOT mentioned in Constitution — purely created by State legislation, hence states can amend it

concepts.name: Punchhi Commission Recommendations on Governor's Discretionary Powers
key_dimensions: Recommendation to delete 'during pleasure of President' clause and provide fixed tenure with removal only by impeachment
Recommendation against Governors acting as agents of Central government
Specific guidelines on government formation, floor tests, and anti-defection in context of Governor's role
UPSC trap: Punchhi Commission (2010) vs. Sarkaria Commission (1988) — both addressed similar issues with different emphases

concepts.name: Distinction Between Governor's Ordinance Power and President's Ordinance Power
key_dimensions: Article 123 vs. Article 213 — structural similarities but critical differences in scope
Governor cannot promulgate ordinance on matters in State List requiring Presidential assent for a Bill
President can promulgate ordinance on Union List and Concurrent List; Governor only on State List and Concurrent List
UPSC trap: Both require 'immediate action' and 'legislature not in session' — but Governor has additional restriction of Presidential prior instruction for certain subjects

concepts.name: Effect of Ordinance on Existing Laws and its Repugnancy with Central Laws
key_dimensions: An ordinance on Concurrent List subject — same repugnancy rules as State legislation under Article 254
Ordinance can modify or repeal existing Act of State Legislature but cannot override Central law without Presidential assent
If ordinance expires/lapses — transactions done under it and rights/liabilities already accrued remain valid (savings clause)
UPSC trap: Article 213(2)(b) — Legislature can pass a law that validates an ordinance retrospectively, making it an Act

concepts.name: Immunity of Governor (Article 361) in Exercise of Discretionary and Ordinance Powers
key_dimensions: Article 361: Governor not answerable to any court for exercise of his powers and duties
Personal immunity from criminal proceedings during term of office
Civil proceedings with 2-month notice can be brought for personal acts but NOT for official acts
UPSC trap: Immunity under Article 361 does NOT mean ordinances/actions are beyond judicial review — the action can be challenged, not the person

concepts.name: Floor Test and Governor's Discretion to Order It
key_dimensions: Composite Floor Test vs. Simple Floor Test — Governor's choice and judicial guidance
G. Pattabhiram Reddy case and Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016): Governor cannot arbitrarily summon assembly
Shivraj Singh Chouhan v. Speaker (2020): Supreme Court on urgency of floor test — Governor can direct it
UPSC trap: Governor ordering floor test is discretionary power but courts can intervene if used malafide or to destabilize legitimate government

concepts.name: Governor's Special Responsibilities Under Constitutional Provisions
key_dimensions: Special responsibilities under Fifth Schedule (tribal areas administration) — Governor has real discretionary role
Sixth Schedule areas — different framework; Governor has specific powers regarding district councils
Article 371 and related articles: Special responsibilities for certain states (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, etc.)
UPSC trap: In special responsibility cases, Governor acts in his PERSONAL JUDGMENT — not on Council of Ministers advice
